Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 Corinthians 1, based on what the requested sites say.

---

## 1 Corinthians 1: Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — "Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul opens with the conventional ancient letter format: sender first, then recipient. He immediately asserts his apostolic credentials — not by human appointment but "by the will of God" — because his authority was being questioned in Corinth. The Greek literally reads "a called apostle" (*kletos apostolos*); Paul is on par with the Twelve because, like them, he was chosen directly by God, not by men (Robertson, cited in both sources). The double emphasis ("called" and "by the will of God") reinforces that his apostleship is divine in origin, not self-assumed.

Sosthenes is likely the former synagogue ruler of Corinth mentioned in Acts 18:17, who was beaten before Gallio's tribunal. Having been converted, he was now with Paul in Ephesus, perhaps serving as his amanuensis (scribe). Paul calls him "our brother," not "apostle," maintaining the distinction in office while acknowledging him as a fellow believer.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 2 — "To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy…"

**Traditional Reading**

The Greek word *ekklesia* was a secular term for an "assembly" of citizens. Paul qualifies it as "the church *of God*" — God's assembly, not the world's. This echoes Old Testament usage in the Septuagint where Israel is called God's assembly.

"Sanctified in Christ Jesus" and "called to be holy" (literally "called saints") describe believers not by their performance but by their position in Christ. Gill notes this sanctification includes election, justification, and the Spirit's ongoing work. The Corinthians had many moral failures, yet Paul addresses them as "saints" — their identity rests on God's promise, not their track record.

The phrase "both their Lord and ours" emphasizes the common Lordship of Christ, laying groundwork for Paul's coming appeal for unity.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 3 — "Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ"

**Traditional Reading**

A standard Pauline greeting blending Greek ("grace," *charis*) and Jewish ("peace," *shalom*) customs. Lenski (cited at Enduring Word) notes: "Grace is always first, peace always second… grace is the source of peace." Gill adds that this salutation is "usual in all Paul's epistles," invoking both the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ equally as the source of divine blessing — an implicit Trinitarian affirmation.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 4 — "I always thank my God for you because of the grace He has given you in Christ Jesus"

**Traditional Reading**

Before any rebuke, Paul expresses sincere gratitude. He thanks God (not the Corinthians' own merit) for the grace given them. Gill notes this includes "all sorts of grace — adopting, justifying, pardoning, regenerating, and sanctifying grace," all coming "through the hands of Christ." Paul models that even a deeply troubled church warrants thanksgiving for what God has genuinely done in it.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary

---

### v. 5 — "For in Him you have been enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge"

**Traditional Reading**

The Corinthians' enrichment is "in Him" (Christ), not from their own resources. "All speech" (*logos*) and "all knowledge" (*gnosis*) likely refer both to their eloquence in proclaiming the gospel and their understanding of Christian truth. Gill notes these included "the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, so as to speak with divers tongues." The Corinthians were genuinely gifted in word and understanding — their problem was not lack of gifts but misuse of them.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 6 — "because our testimony about Christ was confirmed in you"

**Traditional Reading**

The gospel ("testimony of Christ") was validated among the Corinthians. Gill explains this confirmation came through signs and miracles attending the preaching, through the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, and through the internal power of the Spirit applying the gospel to their souls. The changed lives and spiritual gifts among them were evidence that Paul's message was true.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary

---

### v. 7 — "Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ"

**Traditional Reading**

The Corinthian church lacked no *charisma* (spiritual gift). They had the full range of manifestations. Yet Gill adds a pastoral warning: gifts will cease at Christ's coming, and all must give account for how they were used, so they "should be diligently made use of, and improved to the interest and service of Christ." Enduring Word notes Paul thanks God for the gifts even though they were causing trouble — the gifts weren't the problem; wrong attitudes about them were.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

**Denominational Differences**

This verse is significant in Pentecostal and charismatic teaching. Enduring Word (David Guzik, broadly charismatic) emphasizes that spiritual gifts are real and good — the Corinthians' error was not in having them but in carnal attitudes toward them. The non-cessationist reading sees this as affirming that all the gifts continue and that churches should eagerly desire them.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 8 — "He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ"

**Traditional Reading**

Gill specifies that the One who confirms is God the Father (not Christ), since the confirmation is "in Christ" and looks toward the day of Christ. This speaks of perseverance: God will establish them in grace, preserve them in faith and holiness "unto the end," and present them blameless — not sinlessly perfect in themselves, but justified by Christ's righteousness and washed in His blood.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

**Denominational Differences**

Reformed teaching (Ligonier, Desiring God) sees here the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints: God Himself guarantees that those truly called will be kept to the end. This is not based on human effort but on divine faithfulness. The "blameless" presentation at the day of Christ is grounded in justification, not personal sinlessness.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/1-corinthians/1
- https://learn.ligonier.org/scripture/1-corinthians-1

---

### v. 9 — "God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful"

**Traditional Reading**

The ground of the believer's confidence is God's faithfulness, not human steadfastness. "Fellowship" (*koinonia*) means a shared life with Christ. Precept Austin, citing Ray Stedman, calls this "the key verse of First Corinthians" — the Corinthians' problems stemmed from not understanding the implications of their calling into intimate relationship with Jesus Christ.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 10 — "I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together…"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul shifts from thanksgiving to plea. Though he had apostolic authority to command, he "pleads" (*parakalo*) — a loving entreaty rather than a heavy-handed directive. "Divisions" translates *schismata*, meaning "tears or rents" — the body is being ripped apart. "Perfectly joined together" is a medical term (Barclay, cited at Enduring Word) for knitting fractured bones or resetting a dislocated joint. The unity Paul seeks is in "mind" (*nous*) and "judgment" (*gnome*) — both thought and practical decision-making.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary

---

### v. 11 — "My brothers, some from Chloe's household have informed me that there are quarrels among you"

**Traditional Reading**

Chloe was likely a Christian woman (possibly from Corinth or Ephesus) whose household members or business representatives travelled between the two cities and brought Paul news of the strife. "Quarrels" (*erides*) suggests contentious strife, not merely polite disagreement.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 12 — "Individuals among you are saying, 'I follow Paul,' 'I follow Apollos,' 'I follow Cephas,' or 'I follow Christ'"

**Traditional Reading**

Four factions are identified. The "Paul party" claimed loyalty to the church's founder. The "Apollos party" gravitated toward the eloquent Alexandrian preacher (Acts 18:24–28). The "Cephas (Peter) party" looked to the chief of the Twelve. The "Christ party" may have claimed spiritual superiority, disdaining all human leaders. Enduring Word notes Paul may be "changing the names to protect the innocent" (see 1 Cor 4:6), applying to himself and Apollos what was really about local leaders. Regardless, the real boasting was self-congratulation for following a particular leader.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 13 — "Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?"

**Traditional Reading**

Three piercing rhetorical questions expose the absurdity of factionalism. Christ is one; His body cannot be partitioned. Only Christ was crucified for them; no human leader died for their sins. Baptism is into Christ's name, not any apostle's. The questions refocus the Corinthians on the exclusive sufficiency of Christ.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/shameful-cross-vs-proud-eloquence

---

### v. 14–16 — "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius…"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul is thankful he baptized so few, lest anyone claim baptism "in Paul's name." Crispus was the former synagogue ruler (Acts 18:8). Gaius was Paul's host in Corinth (Rom 16:23). The household of Stephanas (1 Cor 16:15–17) was also baptized by Paul. His aside — "beyond that I do not remember" — is not a lapse of inspiration but an honest human recollection, showing that baptism was not Paul's primary focus.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 17 — "For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power"

**Traditional Reading**

This verse does not denigrate baptism (Paul clearly practised it and taught its importance, Rom 6:3–4). Rather, it clarifies Paul's primary commission: gospel proclamation. His distinctive calling was not to be the administrator of the ordinance but the herald of the message. "Not with words of wisdom" introduces the theme of 1:18–2:5: human eloquence and philosophy can actually "empty" (*kenoō*) the cross of its power if they become the basis of faith rather than the message itself.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

---

### v. 18 — "For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God"

**Traditional Reading**

The verb tenses matter: "are perishing" and "are being saved" are both present participles describing ongoing processes. Every person is moving in one direction. The cross divides humanity into two groups: those who see it as absurdity (*moria*) and those who experience it as God's dynamic power (*dynamis*). John Piper notes that the "word of the cross" *is* the gospel — you cannot preach the gospel without preaching Christ crucified. Preaching morality, God's fatherhood, or the brotherhood of man without the cross is not gospel preaching.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

---

### v. 19 — "For it is written: 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate'"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14 (LXX). God actively opposes human wisdom in spiritual matters — He does not bow to it but destroys it. The quotation anchors Paul's argument in Old Testament prophecy: God always intended to bypass human intellectual achievement in His plan of salvation.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 20 — "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age?"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul echoes Isaiah 33:18 and 19:12, taunting worldly wisdom. "The wise man" represents Greek philosophy; "the scribe" represents Jewish learning; "the philosopher" (*suzetetes*, "disputer/debater") represents the skilled rhetorician. All three have been made foolish by God through the cross.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 21 — "For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe"

**Traditional Reading**

Human wisdom, left to itself, failed to find God. This was part of God's wise plan — He permitted human wisdom to exhaust itself so that salvation would come through the "foolishness" (*moria*) of the kerygma (the preached message). The means of salvation is not intellectual discovery but believing response to proclamation. God's pleasure ("God was pleased") is in saving "those who believe," not those who figure it out.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm

---

### v. 22 — "Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom"

**Traditional Reading**

The two great cultural responses to the gospel are identified. Jews wanted miraculous authentication — a sign from heaven validating the messenger. Greeks (Gentiles) wanted intellectual coherence — a system of ideas that made sense by their philosophical standards. Both demands, in their own way, sidestep the scandal of the cross.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 23 — "But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles"

**Traditional Reading**

To the Jew, a crucified Messiah was a contradiction: Deuteronomy 21:23 says "anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse." A cursed Messiah was unthinkable — hence a *skandalon* (stumbling block). To the Greek, the idea that salvation comes through the brutal execution of a Galilean peasant was intellectually absurd — *moria* (foolishness). Paul refuses to adjust the message to suit either audience. He preaches "Christ crucified" anyway.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

---

### v. 24 — "But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God"

**Traditional Reading**

The "called" (*kletoi*) — those effectually summoned by God — perceive what the world misses. To them, the crucified Christ is not weakness but power, not folly but wisdom. Notice the reversal: the Jews wanted power (signs) and the Greeks wanted wisdom; in Christ, both receive exactly what they sought, but in a form that humbles their previous categories. Precept Austin notes that *kletos* is a key word in chapter 1 (occurring in vv. 1, 2, and 24), tying together Paul's call, the Corinthians' call, and the effectual call of all believers.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary

---

### v. 25 — "For the foolishness of God is wiser than man's wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man's strength"

**Traditional Reading**

This is an ironic concession: even if (impossibly) there were "foolishness" or "weakness" in God, it would still surpass the highest human wisdom and strength. The point is that what the world calls foolish (the cross) is in fact the supreme display of divine wisdom; what the world calls weak (Christ crucified) is the supreme display of divine power.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 26 — "Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul turns from the message to the messengers — the Corinthians themselves. "Consider" (*blepete*) means "look at, observe." Their own composition proves God's method: few were intellectuals, few were influential, few were aristocrats. The three categories (wise, powerful, well-born) correspond to the Greco-Roman status markers. God did not recruit the elite.

John Piper notes that this verse reveals why human wisdom is hostile to the cross: at its root is pride. God deliberately bypasses the world's elite to ensure no one may boast before Him (v. 29).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

---

### vv. 27–28 — "But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things… the lowly and despised things… the things that are not, to nullify the things that are"

**Traditional Reading**

God's deliberate strategy is outlined in three escalating pairs:
1. Foolish things → shame the wise
2. Weak things → shame the strong
3. Lowly/despised/"things that are not" → nullify "things that are"

"The things that are not" (*ta me onta*) may echo the philosophical language of being and non-being — God uses what the world considers nothing to render ineffective what the world considers something. The purpose is not that weakness is inherently virtuous, but that human pride is stripped away. Enduring Word: "No one will stand before God and declare, 'I figured You out.'"

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 29 — "so that no one may boast in His presence"

**Traditional Reading**

This is the ultimate purpose of God's upside-down method of salvation: the elimination of all human boasting before God. Piper argues that pride is the root reason human wisdom rejects the cross — the cross humiliates human achievement, and proud people cannot accept that.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

---

### v. 30 — "It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption"

**Traditional Reading**

Everything the believer has is "because of Him" (God the Father) and "in Christ Jesus." Christ Himself *became* wisdom for us — not merely that He teaches wisdom, but that He is our wisdom personified. This wisdom is unpacked in three dimensions:
- **Righteousness** (*dikaiosyne*): justification — Christ's righteousness credited to us.
- **Holiness** (*hagiasmos*): sanctification — being set apart and progressively made holy in Christ.
- **Redemption** (*apolytrosis*): final deliverance — the full liberation from sin and death at the consummation.

These are not human achievements but gifts received "in Christ." Enduring Word notes: "True wisdom isn't about 'getting smart.' God's wisdom is received in and through the person of Jesus."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/

---

### v. 31 — "Therefore, as it is written: 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord'"

**Traditional Reading**

Paul quotes Jeremiah 9:23–24. After systematically dismantling every ground of human boasting — pedigree, intellect, status, achievement — he leaves only one legitimate boast: boasting in the Lord. This is not self-congratulation but grateful exultation in what God has done. The chapter ends where it began: all glory belongs to God, and all good comes through Christ.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-1-commentary

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Emphases

**Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier, Desiring God):** Strong emphasis on the sovereignty of God in calling (vv. 1, 9, 24, 26–29), the doctrine of perseverance (v. 8 — God sustains to the end), and the antithesis between human pride and God's glory (vv. 29–31). The cross is the demonstration that salvation is entirely of God, eliminating all human boasting.

- https://learn.ligonier.org/scripture/1-corinthians-1
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wisdom-of-men-and-the-power-of-god

**Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon cited at Enduring Word, Piper at Desiring God):** Gill emphasizes sovereign election ("sanctified in Christ by election") and the effectual call. Spurgeon, cited at Enduring Word, warns that gifts without consecration are worthless: "Gifts are nothing, unless they are laid on the altar of God." Piper stresses the cross as the exclusive content of saving faith and the danger of "wisdom of men" corrupting genuine faith.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/ (citing Spurgeon)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Affirms that spiritual gifts are real, good, and given by God (v. 7). The Corinthian problem was not the presence of gifts but carnal attitudes. The chapter is read as calling believers to be both "Christocentric" and "Crosscentric" — the cure for division and pride is keeping eyes on Jesus, not suppressing the supernatural.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-1/
